knowledge_type_note: Motif (D). A named special case of zwischenzug rather than an independent geometric pattern.
definition_short: A piece already doomed sells itself as dearly as possible before it is lost.
definition_long:
When a piece is going to be lost regardless, it takes something on the way out, or forces a concession, instead of being captured for nothing. Common in capture races where both sides have hanging pieces, and in stalemate defences.

Formally a special case of the zwischenzug: the doomed piece acts before the expected recapture. Chess.com classifies it that way explicitly.

history.notes: Tactical motifs are descriptive pattern names of long and mostly anonymous usage. The Chess Informant classification is cited as a standard enumeration, not as the origin of the term.

preconditions: A friendly piece cannot be saved
That piece has a capture or forcing move available
indicators_for: Both sides have loose pieces at once
The doomed piece can capture something defended, evening the material count
indicators_against: The piece can actually be saved, in which case desperado logic is simply a blunder

typical_plans: Before conceding a piece, list every capture it can make and every check it can give
In a capture race, count who runs out of desperados first rather than who is ahead now
In a lost position, look for a desperado that reaches stalemate rather than one that wins material
typical_moves: A doomed rook taking a defended pawn on the seventh before being captured
A hanging queen giving itself up for a rook rather than for nothing
A trapped bishop taking the pawn that trapped it
typical_piece_arrangements: Both sides with a hanging piece at once, so the side to move decides the order
A piece attacked with every retreat square covered
tactical_consequences: A desperado inverts normal move ordering: the piece acts before the recapture rather than after, which is why chess.com classifies it as a special case of the zwischenzug
The size of the gain is not the value of what is taken, it is the difference between taking and not taking - which can be several pawns even when the capture is an even trade
strategic_consequences: In stalemate defences a desperado is a way to shed material deliberately, so material counting reads it backwards

exceptions: The whole idea rests on the piece being genuinely unsaveable. Verify that first.
A desperado that gives the opponent a tempo they needed is worse than losing the piece quietly.
If the piece can be saved by a counter-threat rather than by moving, it is not doomed and the desperado is a blunder.
limitations: There is no matcher. 'Cannot be saved' is a claim about every legal move the piece has and about what happens after each, which is a search rather than a static test, and the record's own exception says the first thing to do is verify it.

The example on this record was FOUND rather than constructed, by scanning the 788 shipped puzzles for a solution move where the moving piece could already be won before the move and could still be won on its destination. Fifty positions match that shape. Four hand-built minimal positions were thrown away first: trapping a piece with no escape square needs a cage of enemy men, and every small version left the piece a flight square.

examples.note: Shipped puzzle en-a9ff7ebd22, and it is the record's two preconditions on a real board. THE PIECE CANNOT BE SAVED: the white rook on e1 is attacked down the e-file by the rook on e4 and is defended by nothing - the king on g2 does not reach it and the rook on f2 does not either. IT HAS A CAPTURE AVAILABLE: Rxe4, which is answered by fxe4, so the rook does not survive that either. What makes it a desperado rather than a trade is the alternative: retreating scores -4.93 and taking scores +2.55, a gap of 748 centipawns, because the rook that is going to be lost anyway takes a rook with it and the b7 pawn then decides. Found by scanning all 788 shipped puzzles for a solution move where the moving piece was ALREADY losable before the move and is losable on its destination too - fifty positions match that shape and this is the clearest.

engine.verdict_note: +2.55 for the desperado against -4.93 and -4.99 for the two best rook retreats, at depth 24 with three lines. The margin is the concept: a piece that is lost either way is worth exactly what it can take on the way out, and here that is 748 centipawns.

ambiguous_examples.note: Shipped puzzle en-4ea9212492. The white rook on e6 is attacked down the file by the rook on e3 and is defended by nothing, and Black's e2 pawn is one square from queening - so the rook is going regardless. It takes the black rook on the way out, is recaptured by the king, and both sides queen: 0.00. Filed as ambiguous because the concept delivers precisely what it promises and the result is a draw. This record's positive example is worth 748 centipawns over the alternative; here the desperado is also the best move on the board and is worth the difference between losing and holding, which is a kind of value the definition - 'sells itself as dearly as possible' - does not describe.

engine.verdict_note: 0.00 at depth 22, settled at depth 3, and the desperado is the engine's first choice. Both sides promote and the queens hold each other.

by_level.beginner: This piece is lost anyway, so it grabs something before it goes.
by_level.intermediate: A desperado: since the piece cannot be saved, it takes material on its way off the board.
by_level.advanced: Desperado, a special case of zwischenzug. Confirm the piece really is unsaveable before applying the logic.
